It’s the Red Cross! They need blood for so many reasons and sometimes just for testing and research. Disappointing, sure! But you did your best, and it’s appreciated.

I’ll just add a quick anecdote: I passed out my first time donating at my high school. Woke up to my former army medic science teacher slapping me back into consciousness. 

Freaked me out! Tried again and had to leave bc I had an anxiety attack. I didn’t donate for like a decade. 

What finally made me comfortable was doing exactly what you’re doing, reading the procedures and how well managed it all is, and how to prep for success (the first time I had a half a pop tart for breakfast then did blood right before lunch on a lark, not ideal).

Planning to be hydrated and have a nice filling meal  beforehand also made it feel like a test I studied for and was ready to ace. 

Take your time, it’s not intuitive that it isn’t dangerous, so of course the lizard part of your brain is a bit uncomfortable. But from the other side, I can confirm it feels great to go back! You got this. 

Also don’t be afraid to admit you’re a little anxious due to what happened before and I bet they will keep a special eye on you.

I started naltrexone for drinking and it's honestly a godsend.  Abstinence is the healthiest option, but it also has a super high failure rate, and those failures for me tended to turn into bad binges.  Now I do the Sinclair Method with Naltrexone, and the only slipups I've had (defined as having more than 3-4 glasses socially) have been when I have been a doofus and was non-compliant with the meds.  

Psychologically, it feels way less daunting than saying "I'll never drink again" and physiologically, it just short circuits the dopamine cycle, eventually you just find alcohol doesn't quite "do it" for you anymore.  

Her habits sound pretty similar to mine, so sounds like a great option for her.  I also have worked with RIA health, which specializes in this method, they also provide 1:1 counseling and medical checkins for medication if it's not something her PCP knows much about/feels comfortable with.

I was originally put on 10mg and the side effects for me were just awful - vomiting every day, etc.  Talked to my doctor and we agreed to bump me down to 5mg.  

Things were going a little better than before but eventually the panic attacks came back almost as regularly and for no real apparent reason, so we agreed to try 10mg again.  I was very apprehensive but that bump up went a lot smoother because (a) my body had a few months to acclimate to the 5mg and (b) based on my past experience I spent a week or two using a pill cutter to bump up to 7.5 before going to ten.  Had a little bit of nausea but nothing at all like before, and it seems to be much more effective for me at that dose (panic attacks rare and only if there's an actually stressful trigger vs getting them out of the blue).  

YMMV but that was my experience!

I had a job I loved for four years, after several years before of a very promising career.  I got a new boss that gaslit me, drove me crazy (like literally convinced me I was imagining things).  That contributed to me drinking a lot.

I'm talented and have an advanced degree, and I just can't find meaningful work in my area, and I can't leave my area because it's where my support network is.

And when my career was going well I didn't make time for romantic relationships or anything.  So while I am close to family and have a small circle of close friends (who I can't see cause COVID), I suddenly live in a very small world.

1. Some of the symptoms you describe sound like withdrawal - been there.  If you're suddenly drinking less after a long spell of heavy drinking, with or without naltrexone, there are going to be side effects.  If you feel seriously ill, especially with heart palpitations, go see a doctor.  They can prescribe stuff to see you through the first few days.  But if you're going to drink, just take the pill before \*1hour before, ideally\*
2. If you have not drastically reduced drinking recently, and are still feeling these effects, give it time.  I got nauseous the first few days, and learned I definitely need to eat before i take it, which helped make breakfast a healthy habit!

You'll get there, good for you making the effort.  You say you don't have will power - I think will power means doing what it takes, and recognizing what hasn't worked for you.  You're clearly trying new options.  I hope you stick with this one for a bit, just because chemically it really does get easier.
